h: Glasgow's oldest corner, all in one stroll
p: St Mungo is Glasgow's founder and patron saint, and this part of the city is where its story began. The museum opened in 1993, built in a style that echoes the old Bishop's Castle that once stood here, so it looks older than it is.

Glasgow Cathedral, just across the square, is the real neighbourhood heavyweight. It is one of the very few medieval cathedrals in mainland Scotland to have survived the Reformation largely intact, and the lower church, built over the site of St Mungo's tomb, has an atmosphere all of its own.

Behind the cathedral rises the Glasgow Necropolis, a Victorian garden cemetery packed with grand monuments on a hill. The views back over the cathedral and the city are cracking, and it is a fascinating walk for anyone who likes Victorian history or impressive stonework.

Across the road is Provand's Lordship, one of the oldest houses in Glasgow, dating from the 15th century. It is small, but it gives you a glimpse of what medieval Glasgow might have looked like, and there is a pretty little garden behind it.

Allow an hour or so for the museum itself, and a couple more if you are taking in the cathedral, Necropolis and Provand's Lordship too. As you head back towards the centre down the High Street, look out for the giant mural of St Mungo, part of the city's colourful mural trail. You will soon be in the Merchant City, with its restaurants, bars and handsome old buildings.
